analogy.p: Imagine a family that needs more water. They could connect to a huge pipeline from a distant reservoir (a large-scale transfer: plenty of water but expensive and it changes the land somewhere else), or install a water butt and fix a dripping tap (small-scale, cheap, local, but limited). A sustainable approach asks whether the water will still be there for the children in thirty years and whether neighbours pay the cost. The analogy breaks down because real resource decisions involve whole countries, many competing users, climate change and shared rivers, so one family's choice is far simpler.
analogy.t: A household water butt and the whole-street tap

bullets: You need an **overview** of the strategies for your chosen resource, and a **named, located case study** of a large-scale scheme or a local scheme (check your teacher's case study notes for exact names, dates and figures).

You need to understand the difference between simply **increasing supply** (getting more of the resource) and doing it **sustainably** (without harming people, money or the environment in the long term).
You must be able to **compare strategies**: large-scale and top-down against small-scale and bottom-up.
You should be able to give **advantages and disadvantages** of each strategy for people, the economy and the environment.
Questions often come with a **resource booklet** (figure, graph or table), so practise using data to support your answer.
Remember the link to the rest of the topic: you studied global **supply, demand and resource insecurity** first; strategies are the response to a **deficit**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: In the AQA 'challenge of resource management' topic you study ONE resource in depth: food, water or energy. For that resource you must know the strategies that can **increase supply**, and you must be able to judge which of them are **sustainable**. This note covers all three resources so that you can revise whichever one your school taught, and so that you can see the common pattern behind them. The command words in this part of Paper 2 are usually 'Explain', 'Assess' or 'Evaluate', so you need to give reasons and make a judgement, not just list methods.

bullets: **Sustainable** means it can carry on in the long term without using up the resource or damaging the environment.
**Environmental**: low pollution, low carbon emissions, soil and water protected, habitats kept.
**Economic**: affordable to build and to run, creates jobs, the benefit lasts for decades.
**Social**: meets basic needs, benefits are shared fairly, local communities have a say.
A strategy can **increase supply but not be sustainable**, for example pumping groundwater faster than rain refills it.
A strategy can be **sustainable but small**, for example a village rainwater scheme that is cheap, safe and lasting but supplies only a few hundred people.
Always use the **time frame**: short-term gain against long-term cost is the most common evaluation point.
core.h: What 'sustainable' means and how to test it
core.p: The standard definition is development that **meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**. When you judge a supply strategy you can test it against three headings: **environmental** (does it protect soil, water, air, wildlife and the climate?), **economic** (can it be built and run affordably, and does it provide jobs and income for a long time?) and **social** (does it meet the basic needs of all groups fairly, and are local people involved?). A strategy is only really sustainable if it does reasonably well on all three, and the best answers say clearly which test it passes or fails. Figure 1 shows the three tests.

bullets: **Irrigation**: canals, pumps, sprinklers or drip pipes. Gives more reliable harvests and more crops per year, but can lead to **salinisation** (salts build up in the soil as water evaporates) and uses a lot of water.
**Hydroponics**: no soil is needed, so crops can be grown in deserts, cities or greenhouses; water is recycled so there is less waste; but it needs electricity, nutrients and skilled management.
**Aeroponics**: roots hang in the air and are misted with nutrient solution; uses very little water and no soil, but is expensive and the equipment can fail.

**Biotechnology / GM crops**: higher yields, pest resistance and drought tolerance; but seeds are expensive, farmers may depend on big companies, and some people worry about effects on wildlife and health.
**Fertilisers and pesticides**: raise yields but can pollute rivers (**eutrophication**) and harm wildlife such as bees.
**Mechanisation** (machinery): saves time and labour and covers more land, but needs fuel and capital.
**Appropriate technology** (simple, low-cost, locally maintained equipment such as treadle pumps) suits poorer farmers better than expensive high-tech systems.
core.h: Food: strategies to increase food supply
core.p: The aim of these strategies is to produce more food from the same land or from land that cannot normally be farmed. **Irrigation** is the artificial supply of water to crops, which allows farming in dry areas and lets farmers grow more than one crop per year. **Hydroponics** grows plants in nutrient-rich water with no soil, and **aeroponics** grows them with their roots hanging in air and sprayed with a nutrient mist. **Biotechnology**, including **genetically modified (GM) crops**, changes the genes of a crop so it grows faster, resists pests or tolerates drought. **New technology** such as tractors, fertilisers and pesticides raises yields per hectare. Each one increases supply but each has costs.

bullets: **Organic farming**: less chemical pollution and better soil life; yields are often lower and prices higher.
**Permaculture**: little need for outside inputs once established, and good for wildlife; needs a lot of knowledge and time to set up.
**Urban farming**: fresh food close to customers, uses unused space, reduces transport emissions; limited space, and can be costly per tonne produced.
**Local sourcing**: fewer food miles, support for local farmers; limited choice and seasonal.
**Reducing waste** (better storage, refrigeration, roads and markets): helps especially where much food rots before it reaches consumers.
**Soil conservation** (terracing, cover crops, contour ploughing) keeps soil fertile for future farmers.
**Fair trade** schemes give farmers a better price so they can invest in their land.
core.h: Food: sustainable ways to increase supply
core.p: Sustainable food strategies try to grow enough food while looking after soil, water and wildlife. **Organic farming** avoids artificial fertilisers and pesticides and uses compost, manure and crop rotation. **Permaculture** designs farms to copy natural ecosystems, with mixed crops, trees and animals supporting one another. **Urban farming** (rooftop gardens, allotments, vertical farms) grows food close to the people who eat it. **Local food sourcing** shortens supply chains, so there are fewer **food miles** and money stays in the local economy. **Reducing food waste** is also a way to increase the amount available without producing any more.

bullets: **Where and why**: a dry area with plenty of sunshine but low rainfall; greenhouses control temperature and water so crops grow all year.
**What was done**: plastic greenhouses, drip irrigation, hydroponics and a large export industry.
**Economic benefits**: jobs, export income and a lot of food produced from a small area.
**Social issues**: many workers are migrants, and concerns have been raised about pay and living conditions.
**Environmental problems**: heavy use of groundwater, plastic waste and pollution from agricultural chemicals.
**Judgement**: high output and jobs, but the water use is hard to sustain in a dry area unless the water is managed carefully.
**Local scheme alternative**: if your case study is a small scheme in a low-income country, use the same headings, and stress that local people were involved and it was cheap and easy to maintain.
core.h: Food case study: how to build a 'large-scale agricultural development' answer
core.p: If you study food, you need a case study of a named scheme. Use a clear framework: **where** it is, **what** was done, **why** it was needed, then **benefits** and **problems**, and finally a **judgement**. A well-known example is the **Almería** region of south-east Spain, where tens of thousands of hectares of plastic greenhouses use **drip irrigation** and, in many cases, **hydroponics** to grow vegetables in a dry climate for export to northern Europe. Check your own class notes for the exact case study and figures set by your teacher, and use those first.

bullets: **Dams and reservoirs**: reliable store of water and HEP, flood control; but villages and farmland are flooded, sediment collects behind the dam, and there is less water downstream.
**Water transfers**: bring water to where demand is high; but are costly to build and may cause conflict between the regions involved.
**Desalination**: effectively unlimited sea water; but it uses large amounts of energy, is expensive and produces concentrated brine that harms marine life.
**Groundwater abstraction**: cheap and quick; but if the water is removed faster than it is recharged, water tables fall and wells run dry (an unsustainable use).
**Aquifer**: porous rock that stores groundwater; **recharge** is the natural refilling by rainfall.
**Water conflict**: rivers that cross borders can cause disagreements when one country builds a dam or takes more than its share.
Large projects are usually **top-down** (planned by governments and funded by big loans), whereas small schemes are **bottom-up**.
core.h: Water: strategies to increase water supply
core.p: Water supply can be increased by storing more, moving it, or creating new sources. **Dams and reservoirs** store rainfall from wet seasons for use in dry ones and can also produce **hydro-electric power (HEP)**. **Water transfers** move water from an area with a **surplus** to an area with a **deficit** through pipes, canals or tunnels. **Desalination** removes salt from sea water, either by distillation (boiling and condensing) or by **reverse osmosis** (forcing water through a membrane). **Groundwater abstraction** takes water from aquifers using wells and boreholes. Each has big costs: money, energy, land or damage to ecosystems.

bullets: **Fixing leaks**: in many cities a big share of treated water is lost from old pipes before it reaches homes, so repairs are an effective way to 'create' supply.
**Metering and pricing**: people use less if they pay by volume.
**Grey water recycling**: reduces demand for clean drinking-quality water.
**Rainwater harvesting**: cheap, can be built by communities with local materials, ideal for appropriate technology schemes.
**Groundwater management**: licences and limits on boreholes allow aquifers to recharge.
**Education**: campaigns that change behaviour cost little.
**Limits**: does not give new water where there is simply none, so large schemes may still be needed.
core.h: Water: sustainable ways to manage and increase supply
core.p: Sustainable water strategies reduce demand and use existing water better. **Water conservation** means using less through leak repair, water-efficient appliances and metering. **Recycling and re-use** treat used water so it can be used again, for example **grey water** (from baths and sinks) for flushing toilets or irrigation. **Rainwater harvesting** collects rain from roofs and stores it in tanks. **Groundwater management** limits how much can be taken so aquifers can recover. **Drip irrigation** and efficient farming reduce the huge amounts used in agriculture. These approaches are cheaper and lower-impact than megaprojects, but they alone may not meet the demand of fast-growing cities.

bullets: **Reason**: Gauteng has high demand from cities and industry but limited local water; Lesotho has a surplus.
**What**: dams, reservoirs, tunnels and a hydro-power station moving water by gravity.
**Benefits for Lesotho**: money from water sales, jobs during construction, HEP, roads and other infrastructure.
**Benefits for South Africa**: secure water for homes and industry in the economic heartland.
**Problems**: communities were moved from flooded valleys, farmland and grazing land were lost, and the project cost a very large sum.
**Environmental**: changed river flows and habitats downstream.
**Judgement**: strong economic gain and water security, but social and environmental costs were large, so it is only partly sustainable.
core.h: Water case study: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
core.p: A well-known water transfer example is the **Lesotho Highlands Water Project**. Lesotho, a mountainous country with high rainfall, has built dams (including **Katse** and **Mohale**) and tunnels that send water to the Vaal river system and then to the dry industrial area around Gauteng in South Africa. Lesotho receives **royalty payments** and electricity from hydro-power, while South Africa receives a reliable water supply. Use it as a model for the structure of any large-scale water case study: location, reasons, what was built, benefits, problems and your judgement. Use the facts from your own teacher's case study if it is a different one.

bullets: **Fossil fuels**: reliable and cheap infrastructure exists; but burning releases CO2 (enhanced greenhouse effect) and reserves are finite.
**Fracking**: extracts gas from shale rock; local concern about earth tremors, water use and pollution risk.
**Nuclear**: very high energy output per kilogram of fuel and no carbon dioxide when generating; but waste stays dangerous for a long time, and an accident would be severe.
**Wind**: no fuel costs and no emissions in operation; but it is intermittent, visual impact, and noise concerns.
**Solar**: good in sunny places, can be small-scale on roofs; but no output at night and the panels are costly to produce.
**HEP**: reliable and controllable; but needs dams and suitable valleys.
**Biomass and biofuels**: can be carbon-neutral if regrown; but land used for fuel crops can reduce land for food.
core.h: Energy: strategies to increase energy supply
core.p: Countries can increase energy supply from **fossil fuels**, **nuclear power** or **renewables**. Exploiting **new fossil fuel reserves** (such as shale gas obtained by hydraulic fracturing, or oil from deep offshore wells) gives more energy but adds to carbon emissions and climate change. **Nuclear power** gives large amounts of electricity with almost no carbon dioxide while operating, but has high building costs and produces radioactive waste. **Renewable sources** (wind, solar, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass) replace fuel that runs out with sources that are naturally replenished.

bullets: **Energy efficiency**: insulation in homes, efficient boilers and lights, public transport; lowers bills and carbon emissions.
**Carbon footprint**: the total greenhouse gases produced by an activity or person; reducing it is a sustainability aim.
**Energy mix**: a balanced mixture of sources makes a country less reliant on one fuel and more energy secure.
**Small-scale schemes**: solar home systems, biogas digesters and micro-hydro; cheap to run, controlled locally, and quick to install.
**Intermittency**: renewables such as wind and solar depend on weather, so storage or back-up supply is needed.
**Carbon capture** (capturing carbon dioxide from power stations): still developing and costly.
**Government role**: subsidies, targets and taxes on carbon can encourage the switch.
core.h: Energy: sustainable ways to increase supply and cut demand
core.p: A sustainable energy strategy increases supply from renewable sources and also reduces how much energy is needed. **Energy conservation** (switching off, better insulation) and **energy efficiency** (modern appliances, LED lighting, efficient vehicles) reduce demand, so the same supply goes further. Combining a varied **energy mix** with some storage and back-up makes supply more secure. In low-income countries, small schemes such as solar panels or small hydro generators can bring power to remote villages without needing a national grid, and they are an example of **appropriate technology**.

bullets: **Large-scale**: high output, high cost, usually government or international funding, longer to build, bigger environmental and social impact.
**Small-scale**: low cost, uses local labour and materials, easy to maintain; limited output.
**Short-term vs long-term**: some strategies fix a problem now but create bigger ones later (for example over-pumping groundwater).
**Who benefits?** Often urban industry gains while rural communities lose land.
**Ownership and maintenance**: schemes that local people manage are more likely to keep working.
**Linking with development**: reliable resources help health, education and economic growth, supporting development.
**Use evidence**: quote figures from the resource booklet or your case study when making a comparison.
core.h: Comparing strategies: scale, cost and who decides
core.p: Examiners reward answers that compare strategies instead of describing each one separately. A useful comparison is **large-scale, top-down** schemes (big dams, nuclear stations, huge irrigation projects) against **small-scale, bottom-up** schemes (rainwater tanks, solar panels, community gardens). Large schemes supply a lot and quickly meet national demand, but cost huge sums, may displace people and often damage ecosystems. Small schemes are cheap, controlled by communities and easy to maintain, but supply less. Often the best long-term answer is a combination.

bullets: **Percentage** = part divided by whole times 100.
**Percentage change** = (new value minus old value) divided by old value times 100.
**Describing a trend**: say whether it increases or decreases, give the start and end values, and mention any anomalies.
**Reading a line graph**: place a ruler on the value and read across to the axis; check the scale and units.
**Reading a pie chart or bar chart**: compare the size of each segment or bar, and use numbers from the labels.
**Using a map**: describe patterns (for example 'concentrated in', 'few in') and name places.
**Quote evidence**: figures from the data are what turn a general statement into a mark-earning point.
core.h: Data and graph skills for this topic
core.p: Paper 2 often gives a graph, table or map and asks you to use it. For supply and demand diagrams, the key ideas are the **gap** between lines (a **deficit** if demand is above supply, a **surplus** if supply is above demand) and **trends** (steepness shows how fast something is changing). For tables of an energy mix or water use you may need to calculate a **percentage**, a **percentage change** or a **mean**. Always include **units**, quote **figures** from the source, and say what the data shows and why. Figure 4 shows how a deficit looks on a graph.

bullets: **Point, Evidence, Explain (PEE)**: make a point, support it with a fact or a place, then explain why it matters.
**Both sides**: give at least one benefit and one problem; examiners reward balance.
**Link to sustainability**: say which of environmental, economic or social tests it passes or fails.
**Scale and time**: mention short-term and long-term effects and who is affected.
**Conclusion**: choose a side ('this is most sustainable because...') and justify it; do not just sit on the fence.
**Use a named example**: a named and located case study often turns a mid-level answer into a top-level one.
**Avoid repetition**: each paragraph should add a new idea.
core.h: How to evaluate and conclude (6 and 9 mark questions)
core.p: Evaluate questions ask you to weigh up advantages and disadvantages and reach a supported conclusion. Use a clear structure: begin with a short definition of what the strategy does, then give developed points about the benefits (with evidence), then the problems, then compare with another option or with the three sustainability tests, and finally give a **justified judgement** that answers the question as it was asked. Figure 5 gives a five-step checklist. For the longer questions, spelling, punctuation and grammar may also be assessed, so write in clear paragraphs with specialist terms spelled correctly.

bullets: **Climate change**: fossil fuel use raises CO2; changing rainfall patterns affect irrigation and water supply.
**Urban issues**: growing cities increase demand for all three resources.
**Development**: poor access to clean water, food and electricity limits health and education.
**Ecosystems**: dams flood habitats; irrigation lowers river levels; wind farms may affect birds.
**Economic activity**: industry needs energy and water; farming needs water.
**Global pattern**: resources are unevenly distributed, so trade and cooperation are needed.
**Future outlook**: population growth and rising incomes will increase demand, so the 'sustainable' tests become more important.
core.p: This topic does not stand alone. The more links you can make, the higher your answers climb. Resource security is tied to **climate change** (fossil fuel use causes warming and warming alters rainfall and crop yields), to **urban growth** (megacities need food, water and energy delivered at huge scale), to **development** (access to resources is part of a country's quality of life), and to **ecosystems** (dams, farms and power stations change habitats). Good links make evaluations richer.

exam: **Describe** = say what you see or what happens; **Explain** = give reasons using 'because' or 'this leads to'; **Assess/Evaluate** = weigh up and reach a judgement.
**1 mark**: one correct fact or definition (for example 'Water moved from an area of surplus to deficit').
**2 marks**: one point developed with a reason (point + because).
**4 marks**: two developed points, or four linked statements; often 'Explain how...' questions.
**6 marks** (levelled): at least two sides, specific evidence and a judgement; use a named case study.
**9 marks** (levelled, with SPaG on some papers): well-developed argument, detailed knowledge, evidence from the resource booklet, and a clear conclusion.
Use **model phrases**: 'This is sustainable because it does not harm future generations by...', 'However, the cost of ... means that...', 'On balance...'.
For graphs: quote **two figures with units**, describe the **trend**, and give a **reason**.
Always name **place**, **scale** (large or small), **who benefits** and **who loses** to reach top levels.
Check the question: is it asking for **increase supply** or **sustainable** or both?
Leave time to **read the resource** and underline command words before writing.

mistakes.r: Sustainable means it meets present needs without harming future generations and considers environmental, economic and social effects.
mistakes.w: 'Sustainable means it lasts a long time.'

mistakes.r: A balanced answer: dams give reliable water and HEP but flood land, move people, trap sediment and reduce flow downstream.
mistakes.w: 'Dams are good because they give water.' (one-sided)

mistakes.r: The supply of sea water is huge, but desalination uses a lot of energy, is expensive and produces salty brine, so it is not usually very sustainable.
mistakes.w: 'Desalination is sustainable because there is lots of sea water.'

mistakes.r: Renewables have lower emissions but can be intermittent, expensive to set up and affect landscapes and wildlife.
Answer about the resource and case study asked for; use named places and figures.
mistakes.w: Writing about food, water and energy all at once in a case study answer.

mistakes.r: Use balanced, factual points: higher yields and resistance against possible concerns about cost, seed dependence and wildlife effects.
mistakes.w: 'GM crops are bad for you.' (unsupported opinion)

mistakes.r: Develop the point: who gets the jobs, how many, for how long, and what that means for local income.
mistakes.w: Saying 'it creates jobs' with no further explanation.

mistakes.r: Finish with a conclusion that answers the question and is supported by evidence.
mistakes.w: Describing a strategy with no judgement.

mistakes.r: Conservation is using less; recycling is treating used resource so it can be used again.

summary: The specification asks you to know the strategies for increasing the supply of your chosen resource (food, water or energy) and to judge how sustainable they are, using a named case study. It matters because evaluation questions on Paper 2 are worth many marks and reward balanced arguments with evidence.

The amount of a resource available to be used.
The amount of a resource that people want or use.
A situation where supply is less than demand.
A situation where supply is greater than demand.

Growing plants in nutrient-rich water without soil.

Using living organisms or their genes to make products or improve crops, such as GM crops.

Farming designed to copy natural ecosystems so inputs are low and production lasts.

Removing salt from sea water to make it fit to drink.
An underground layer of porous rock that stores water.

worked.ans: Model answer: Hydroponics grows plants in nutrient-rich water instead of soil, so food can be grown where land is poor or scarce. Plants get all the nutrients they need straight to their roots, so they grow faster and yields are higher. Because the water is recycled, less is wasted, which helps in dry areas. It can also be done in controlled indoor conditions, so crops can be harvested all year, increasing total supply.
worked.q: Explain how hydroponics can increase food supply. (4 marks)
steps: Point 1: plants are grown in nutrient solution so no soil is needed, so crops can be grown in places with poor soil or little land, such as deserts or cities.
Point 2: nutrients are supplied directly to roots, so plants grow faster and yields are higher.
Point 3: water is recycled, so less is wasted, which is useful in dry areas.
Point 4: it can be done indoors, so crops grow all year, giving more harvests.

worked.ans: Model answer: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project moves water from dams in Lesotho, such as Katse and Mohale, to the Gauteng region of South Africa. Economically it is a success because it gives South Africa a reliable water supply for homes and industry, and Lesotho earns royalties and electricity from hydro-power. However, social and environmental costs are significant: communities lost homes and farmland when valleys were flooded, and river flows and habitats downstream have changed. The project also cost a very large sum to build. On balance it is only partly sustainable: it meets present needs and brings income, but the loss of land and ecosystems may harm the future of local people, so it would be more sustainable if combined with water conservation and fair support for affected communities.
worked.q: Evaluate the sustainability of a named large-scale water transfer scheme. (6 marks)
steps: Name and locate: Lesotho Highlands Water Project (or your own case study).
Benefits with evidence: reliable water for the Gauteng region, income and HEP for Lesotho.
Problems with evidence: villages and farmland flooded, huge cost, changed river flows.
Apply the three tests: economic gains, social and environmental costs.
